newsitem.title: PERU: Amid acclaim, Peru faces execution charges.
newsitem.headline: Amid acclaim, Peru faces execution charges.

text.p: Peru, still basking in acclaim for its dramatic rescue of 71 hostages from Marxist rebels, faced accusations on Friday that two of the guerrillas were executed and others were shot as they tried to surrender.

Two male rebels were captured alive during the raid on the Japanese ambassador's residence and shot to death one after the other, according to hostage, police, military and intelligence service sources.
"The order was to leave no one alive. For us, the instruction was to leave no prisoners," said an army commando who took part in Tuesday's assault.

Security force and intelligence sources who monitored the raid said the two captured rebels were summarily killed by shooting. Their reports suggested a possible breach of international practices on the taking of prisoners, committed on what is regarded as Japanese sovereign soil.
The security sources said neither of the executed rebels was Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) leader Nestor Cerpa or his second-in-command Rolly Rojas.
The government has not responded publicly to the reports. But, if proved, they could seriously undercut the praise that Peru's armed forces have won for the raid.
Agriculture Minister Rodolfo Munante, a freed hostage, vehemently denied that he had seen or heard any of the rebels try to surrender before they were killed.

"I have not said that at any time and it seems absolutely absurd," Munante told a news conference. He had been quoted by CBS/Telenoticias television as having described seeing a rebel surrender in the room where captive judges were held.

At least one teenage rebel girl was also shot to death while trying to give herself up, an intelligence agent who monitored the raid via listening devices said. The source said the girl shouted "We surrender! We surrender!" when she was surprised along with at least one other female rebel.

An MRTA member in Lima told Reuters soon after Tuesday's assault that four rebels had been shot by troops despite asking to surrender. "They were the four youngest. They were in a room on their own. They gave up out of fear," said the rebel, who heard the exchange on a short-wave radio.
Military sources said each rebel was given a final "coup de grace" shot in the forehead to make sure they were dead.

Cerpa was shot to death as he ran up a grand staircase. He had been caught off guard playing soccer as commandos exploded through the floor and swarmed out of tunnels dug under the diplomatic mansion. His last words, according to security forces sources, were: "We're screwed, we're screwed."

All 14 rebels, one hostage and two soldiers died in the assault, which rescued 71 men after 126 days in captivity. The MRTA, widely seen as a spent force, still threatened to carry out reprisal attacks in response to the military raid.

"Over the next few days there will be actions carried out all across Peru," Norma Velazco, European spokeswoman for the MRTA, said in an interview published on Friday on the group's Web page Rebel Voice.
The MRTA has barely 200 fighters, mainly in the eastern jungle, and has apparently not taken any armed actions since an earlier threat on Tuesday, just hours after the attack.

President Alberto Fujimori, enjoying one of Peru's greatest triumphs in a 17-year war against leftist guerrillas, toured the burned-out residence later on Thursday with visiting Japanese Foreign Minister Yukihiko Ikeda and wheelchair-bound Japanese Ambassador Morihisa Aoki, the host of the ill-fated Dec. 17 party that was seized by the MRTA.
The whereabouts of the bodies of 12 of the slain MRTA rebels remained a mystery on Friday, although Cerpa and Rojas were privately buried on Thurdsay night by relatives.

"Long live the MRTA. There will be vengeance!" shouted mourners at Rojas' funeral. His body was carried in a wooden coffin through a dusty shantytown graveyard as his mother wept that Fujimori "broke his promise" to end the siege peacefully.

The body of his commander, Cerpa, was buried in a simple wooden coffin covered with earth and stones, and without the traditional cross in this Roman Catholic country. Morgue officials refused to disclose the whereabouts of the other bodies, which were trussed up in black plastic bags and carried out of the gutted residence the day after the raid.

As Fujimori's popularity ratings soared, Japan thanked him officially for the strike in which all 24 Japanese citizens were freed alive. Ikeda told the Peruvian leader his operation was "near-perfect and miraculous."
